title: Persistence and replication
goal: By the end you can say what each persistence setting loses when the Redis process dies and when the whole machine dies, estimate what a fork costs, explain how a replica catches up after a break, and choose RDB, AOF, replication and Sentinel for the Redis that holds lesson 8's idempotency keys.

warmup.q: Redis runs with `appendonly yes` and the default `appendfsync everysec`. A deploy script sends `kill -9` to the Redis process while a service is writing payments. How many acknowledged writes are missing after the restart?
options: About one second of writes: everysec only flushes the log once a second
None: Redis handed each write to the kernel before it replied, and the kernel outlived the process
Everything written since the last RDB snapshot
Only the write whose reply was on its way when the signal arrived
warmup.why: Before Redis sends a reply, it has already passed the logged command to the kernel with `write()`. The kernel keeps those bytes in its page cache and writes them to disk later, and the death of the process can't take them back. In the lab, 8,894 INCRs were acknowledged before the kill and the counter read 8,894 after the restart. The one second of `everysec` is what a crash of the whole machine can lose: power, a kernel panic, a VM that disappears. The last option describes a write that was never acknowledged, so its loss breaks no promise.

sections.h: A restart empties Redis unless a copy of the data left memory
sections.body:
Lesson 8's idempotency records and rate-limit counters live only in Redis, and lesson 5 sized such a store: 3 million keys, about 500 MB, all in RAM. Now the Redis process restarts. A deploy, the OOM killer, a host reboot: it doesn't matter which. The new process starts with nothing, and every payment retried over the next 24 hours finds no key, looks new, and is charged again.

Memory holds the only live copy of the data. Everything in this lesson is a second copy that trails behind it, and you can judge each one with two questions. How far behind memory is it? And what does keeping it current cost lesson 2's single command thread? When the server dies, you lose exactly the writes that hadn't reached a copy yet. That gap is the model for this lesson. The picture below shows the three ways out of memory, and the sections take them in turn.

The simplest copy is a dump: walk every key and write it all to a file. Redis calls it an **RDB file** (Redis database), `dump.rdb`: a compact binary snapshot of the whole dataset at one moment. On restart, Redis loads it before it accepts any client. The command that writes one is `SAVE`.

`SAVE` runs on the main thread, and that is its problem. In the lab, 1,000,000 payments used 83 MB of memory and made a 45 MB file. `SAVE` took 2,065 ms, and a `GET` that another client sent 200 ms after it started waited 1,761 ms for its answer. Nothing else ran in between, because the thread that runs every command was busy writing a file. At 25 GB the same pause would last minutes.

So someone other than the main thread must write the copy, and the copy must still be a consistent picture of one moment. If a thread wrote keys out one by one while clients kept changing them, payment 5 in the file could be from 10:00:00 and payment 900,000 from 10:00:02, with a refund recorded and the payment it refunds missing. The next section shows how Redis gets both properties at once.

try.title: Lose the writes since the last snapshot
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the server if it isn't running: `docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d`. It runs Redis's default persistence: RDB save points and no append-only file. Open a prompt with `docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli` and run the first three commands below.

From a second terminal in the `labs` folder, kill the server process the hard way and start it again: `docker compose -f env/redis.yml kill -s KILL redis`, then `docker compose -f env/redis.yml start redis`. Reconnect and predict what `GET payment:981` returns.
Write the payment again, run `BGSAVE`, and repeat the kill and the start. Predict the second `GET` before you run it.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.src:
CONFIG GET save
SET payment:981 approved
INFO persistence
# kill -9 the server and start it from the second terminal, then reconnect
GET payment:981
SET payment:981 approved
BGSAVE
# kill -9 and start it again, then reconnect
GET payment:981

try.expect: `CONFIG GET save` prints `3600 1 300 100 60 10000`: snapshot after an hour if at least 1 key changed, after 5 minutes if 100 did, after a minute if 10,000 did. `INFO persistence` shows `rdb_changes_since_last_save:1` (more if you wrote other keys since the last snapshot) and `aof_enabled:0`. After the kill, the first `GET` prints `(nil)`: Redis acknowledged the write with `OK` and then lost it, because no snapshot held it yet. `BGSAVE` answers `Background saving started`, and after the second kill `GET` prints `"approved"`. `docker compose -f env/redis.yml logs redis` shows the restart: `Done loading RDB, keys loaded: 1, keys expired: 0.`

sections.h: BGSAVE forks a child, and copy-on-write freezes its view
sections.body:
`BGSAVE` hands the work to a second process. The main thread calls `fork()`, the system call that creates a copy of the calling process. The Operating systems track's lesson on copy-on-write (Copy-on-write, mmap and the OOM killer) showed what that copy really is. The kernel duplicates the page table, the map from the process's addresses to physical memory, so both processes point at the same pages. Nothing is copied until one of them writes to a page. Then the kernel copies that one page, 4 KB, and gives the copy to the writer. That is **copy-on-write**.

It gives Redis exactly the frozen picture it needs. The child sees memory as it was at the instant of the fork, however much the parent changes afterwards. It writes every key to `temp-<pid>.rdb` and then renames that file over `dump.rdb`. A rename is atomic, so a crash halfway through leaves the old snapshot in place, never half of a new one. Meanwhile the parent keeps serving clients.

Two costs remain, and both land on the parent. The fork itself runs on the main thread while the kernel copies the page table, and the page table grows with the data: at 8 bytes per 4 KB page, a 24 GB Redis has 24 GB / 4 KB × 8 = 48 MB of it to copy. The Redis docs list measured fork times (`latest_fork_usec` in `INFO`): about 9 to 13 ms per GB on physical machines and VMware, 10 ms on current EC2 instances, 23 ms on a KVM VM, and 239 ms per GB on older Xen-based EC2 instances, where a 6.1 GB fork stopped the server for 1.46 seconds. The lab's 83 MB forked in 6 to 31 ms. The second cost is the copies: every page the parent writes during the save gets copied. In the demo below, a few hundred updates during one BGSAVE made the kernel copy 3 to 5 MB; 300,000 updates during another copied 27 MB (`rdb_last_cow_size` in `INFO persistence`). On a write-heavy server the worst case is close to twice the memory, which is why `maxmemory` (lesson 5) must stay well below the machine's RAM. Transparent huge pages make it far worse: the kernel then copies a whole 2 MB page on the first write to it, so a few thousand writes can copy almost the whole dataset, and the docs say to turn them off.

You rarely type BGSAVE yourself; the `save` setting runs it. The default `save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000` starts one after 3,600 seconds if at least 1 key changed, after 300 seconds if 100 did, and after 60 seconds if 10,000 did. So the gap on a busy server is about a minute of writes, and on a quiet one up to an hour. For a cache that is fine. For idempotency keys it isn't: a crash undoes every key since the last snapshot, and those are exactly the payments most likely to be retried. Snapshots stay useful anyway. The file is compact, loads quickly (1,000,000 keys in about 1.5 seconds in the lab), and is the natural thing to copy off the machine as a backup.

sections.h: The append-only file logs each write, and fsync decides when it is safe
sections.body:
A snapshot loses minutes. To lose less, record each write as it happens. That is the **append-only file** (AOF): with `appendonly yes`, Redis appends every command that changes data to a log, in the same RESP format clients send (lesson 2), and replays the log on restart. Appending never rewrites old bytes, so a crash can at worst cut off the last command, and Redis drops that half command when it loads.

But writing to a file is not writing to the disk. The Operating systems track's lesson on the page cache (The page cache, writeback and fsync) showed the two steps. `write()` copies bytes into the page cache, the kernel's in-memory copy of file data, and returns at once. The kernel sends those pages to the disk later, within about 30 seconds on Linux. Only `fsync()` makes the device store them, and it waits until it has, often for milliseconds.

That splits "a crash" into two events. If the Redis process dies (kill -9, the OOM killer, a segfault), the kernel keeps running and still holds the page cache, so every byte passed to `write()` reaches the disk. If the machine dies (power, a kernel panic, a cloud VM that vanishes), the page cache dies with it, and only what was fsynced survives.

Redis calls `write()` on the log in the same pass of the event loop, before it sends that pass's replies. `appendfsync` decides when it fsyncs:

| `appendfsync` | when Redis fsyncs | the process dies | the machine dies |
|---|---|---|---|
| `always` | before replying, once per pass | nothing lost | nothing lost |
| `everysec` (default) | once a second, on a background thread | nothing lost | about the last second |
| `no` | never: the kernel decides | nothing lost | up to about 30 seconds |

The lab measures the column for a dying process: under all three policies, kill -9 loses no acknowledged write. `always` pays with speed. In the same 3-second test it got through 1,826 writes, against 8,894 with `everysec`, because every pass waits for the disk; writes from many clients in one pass share one fsync, which helps under load.

The log has one more problem: it only grows. 100,000 `INCR`s on one counter are 100,000 log entries for one number. A rewrite (`BGREWRITEAOF`, started automatically once the log has doubled since the last rewrite and passed 64 MB) forks, and the child writes the current data as a new base file, in RDB format (`aof-use-rdb-preamble yes`). The parent appends new writes to a fresh increment file, and a small manifest lists which files make up the log. Since Redis 7.0 this multi-part AOF lives in its own directory, and Redis swaps the manifest atomically when the child is done.

sections.h: A replica copies the stream of writes, and catches up from a backlog
sections.body:
Files on the same machine don't help when the machine is gone for good, and a restart that loads 25 GB takes minutes. The next copy lives on another server. `replicaof primary 6379` turns a Redis into a **replica**: a read-only copy of a primary that follows every change. The Replication track in the next part builds the general idea, from leaders and followers to what readers see while a copy lags; this section is how Redis does it.

A new replica starts with a full copy. The primary forks, and its child streams a snapshot, the same one BGSAVE would write, straight into the socket (`repl-diskless-sync yes`, the default since 7.0). Meanwhile the primary buffers the writes it keeps receiving. The replica loads the snapshot and applies the buffered writes, and from then on the primary forwards every write to it as RESP: the **replication stream**, nearly the same bytes as the AOF.

The primary replies to its client first and sends to replicas without waiting, so replication is **asynchronous**: a replica is always slightly behind. Each replica reports its position once a second. The position is an offset, a count of every byte of the stream so far (`master_repl_offset` in `INFO replication`). The primary also has a replication ID, a random 40-character name for its history. The pair (ID, offset) names one exact version of the data: two servers at the same pair hold the same keys.

Links break: a network blip, a replica restart, a VM frozen for a few seconds. The simplest repair, another full copy, costs a fork and a transfer of the whole dataset after every blip. So the primary keeps the newest part of the stream in memory, the **backlog**, 1 MB by default (`repl-backlog-size`). A replica that reconnects sends `PSYNC <replication ID> <next byte it needs>`. If the ID matches and that byte is still in the backlog, the primary answers `+CONTINUE` and sends only the missing bytes: a partial resync. Otherwise it answers `+FULLRESYNC` and starts over with a snapshot.

In the lab, a replica that missed 100 writes got them in one message of 4,808 bytes. One that missed 20,000 writes, about 1.5 MB, needed byte 25,164 while the backlog began at byte 531,441, so it got a full resync. Size the backlog as write rate times the longest outage you want to ride out: at 2 MB/s of stream, 60 seconds needs 120 MB. Replicas also follow lesson 5's rule on expiry: they never expire keys themselves, and wait for the primary's DEL.

frames.say: So the primary answers `+FULLRESYNC`: it forks, the child streams a full snapshot to the replica (the same copy-on-write snapshot as BGSAVE), and the stream continues from the snapshot's offset. The replica throws its data away and loads the snapshot. On a 25 GB dataset that is minutes of network and a fork, which is why you size the backlog for your longest normal outage.

try.title: Watch a replica continue, then start over
steps: From the `labs` folder, start a primary, a replica and three Sentinels: `docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml up -d --wait`. The alias below saves typing. Read the replication state, write on the primary, read on the replica, and try a write on the replica.
Make a short outage: freeze the replica with `pause`, cut its link from the primary with `CLIENT KILL TYPE replica`, write 100 payments, thaw it with `unpause`, and read the primary's log.

Make a long one: `pause` and `CLIENT KILL` again, then 20,000 payments (about 1.5 MB of stream against a 1 MB backlog), then `unpause`. Predict the log line first. Keep the containers running for the next Try it.

code.title: from the labs folder
code.src:
alias ha='docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml'
ha exec primary redis-cli INFO replication
ha exec primary redis-cli SET payment:981 approved
ha exec replica redis-cli GET payment:981
ha exec replica redis-cli SET payment:982 approved
ha pause replica
ha exec primary redis-cli CLIENT KILL TYPE replica
ha exec primary redis-cli EVAL "for i=1,100 do redis.call('SET','payment:'..i,'approved') end return 100" 0
ha unpause replica; sleep 2
ha logs primary | grep -i resync
# the long outage: pause and CLIENT KILL again, then
ha exec primary redis-cli EVAL "for i=1,20000 do redis.call('SET','payment:'..i,'approved:EUR:1250:merchant-77') end return 20000" 0
ha unpause replica; sleep 8
ha logs primary | grep -i -E 'resync|backlog'
ha exec primary redis-cli INFO stats | grep sync_

try.expect: `INFO replication` shows `role:master`, `connected_slaves:1`, `slave0:ip=replica,port=6379,state=online,offset=433,lag=1`, a 40-character `master_replid` and `repl_backlog_size:1048576`. The replica answers `"approved"`, and its SET fails with `READONLY You can't write against a read only replica.` After the short outage the primary logs `Partial resynchronization request from replica:6379 accepted. Sending 4808 bytes of backlog starting from offset 875.` (your byte counts may differ a little). After the long one: `Unable to partial resync with replica replica:6379 for lack of backlog (Replica request was: 6475).`, then `Full resync requested by replica replica:6379 (rdb-channel)`. The first `Full resync` line in the log is the replica's initial sync. `INFO stats` ends with `sync_full:2`, `sync_partial_ok:1` and `sync_partial_err:1`.

sections.h: WAIT counts the copies, and Sentinel moves the primary
sections.body:
Asynchronous replication leaves a hole. The primary acknowledges a payment and dies a millisecond later, and the replica that takes over never received it. The client was told OK, and the write is gone. The best-known measurement is old: in 2013 Kyle Kingsbury's Jepsen test split a five-node Redis 2.6 with Sentinel and lost 1,126 of 1,998 acknowledged writes, 56%, because both sides of the split had a primary taking writes. Read it as history: that Redis had no `WAIT` (it arrived in 3.0) and an older Sentinel. The property behind it still holds in 2026: replication is asynchronous, and a failover can lose acknowledged writes.

`WAIT 1 500` narrows the hole. It blocks the connection until at least 1 replica has acknowledged every write this connection sent before it, or until 500 ms have passed, and returns how many replicas did. Three details decide whether it helps you. It counts writes made on the same connection, so with Jedis's pooled `RedisClient`, send the SET and the WAIT in one pipeline, which uses one connection (the compare block below does). It undoes nothing: in the lab, with the replica frozen, `WAIT 1 1000` returned `0` after 1.01 seconds, and the payment stayed on the primary for every client to read. And a replica's acknowledgement means "in its memory", not "on its disk". The docs put it plainly: WAIT does not make Redis a strongly consistent store. Treat 0 as "not confirmed yet" and alert or retry, never as "it didn't happen". `WAITAOF 1 1 100` (Redis 7.2) goes further: it waits until the write is fsynced on this server and on one replica.

Someone also has to promote the replica, and a person paged at 3 a.m. is slow. **Sentinel** does it: separate `redis-sentinel` processes, usually three, on three machines. Each one pings the primary. A Sentinel that gets no valid reply for `down-after-milliseconds` (30 seconds by default, 3 in the lab) marks it subjectively down, `+sdown`. When a quorum of Sentinels agree (2 of 3 here), the primary is objectively down, `+odown`. Then a majority of all Sentinels elect one of them to run the failover. It promotes the best replica, points the other replicas at it, and tells everyone the new address. In the lab the switch came about 4 seconds after the primary froze. Clients never hard-code the primary: they ask a Sentinel with `SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name payments`, and ask again when connections fail. Jedis's `RedisSentinelClient` and Lettuce's Sentinel URIs do that for you.

The majority rule is why you run three: the side of a network split with one Sentinel can't promote anything. The isolated old primary can still take writes from clients on its side, though, and those vanish when it rejoins as a replica. `min-replicas-to-write 1` with `min-replicas-max-lag 10` makes a primary refuse writes once no replica has acknowledged anything for 10 seconds, which caps that loss. And the promoted replica keeps the old replication ID as its second ID, so the remaining replicas continue with a partial resync.

try.title: Wait for a frozen replica, then fail over
steps: With `env/redis-ha.yml` still up, open a prompt on the primary: `docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml exec primary redis-cli`. Write a payment and WAIT for one replica.

In a second terminal in the `labs` folder, freeze the replica: `docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml pause replica`. At the prompt, write another payment, WAIT up to a second, and read it back. Predict both answers. Then `unpause replica`.

Now freeze the primary instead (`pause primary`) and follow a Sentinel's log with `docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml logs -f sentinel-1`. When `+switch-master` appears, ask a Sentinel where the primary is: `docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml exec sentinel-1 redis-cli -p 26379 SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name payments`. Then `unpause primary`, wait half a minute, and run `INFO replication` on it. Finish with `docker compose -f env/redis-ha.yml down -v`.

code.title: at the primary's redis-cli prompt
code.src:
SET payment:983 approved
WAIT 1 500
# pause the replica from the second terminal
SET payment:984 approved
WAIT 1 1000
GET payment:984

try.expect: The first `WAIT` prints `(integer) 1` at once. With the replica frozen, `WAIT 1 1000` prints `(integer) 0` and redis-cli shows `(1.01s)`, yet `GET payment:984` prints `"approved"`: nothing was rolled back. After the pause of the primary, the Sentinel log shows `+sdown master payments primary 6379` about 3 seconds later, `+odown master payments primary 6379 #quorum 2/2` (sometimes `3/2`), `+vote-for-leader`, `+selected-slave slave replica:6379`, `+promoted-slave` and `+switch-master payments primary 6379 replica 6379`, about 4 seconds after the pause in my run. `SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name payments` now answers `"replica"` and `"6379"`. About 20 seconds after the unpause the Sentinel logs `+convert-to-slave slave primary:6379`, and the old primary's `INFO replication` says `role:slave` and `master_host:replica`. The new primary's `INFO replication` shows the old ID as `master_replid2`.

analogy: Think of a shop that keeps its live stock count on a whiteboard. Once an hour someone photographs the board: that is the snapshot, and the camera captures one instant even while the staff keep writing. A clerk also notes every change in a notebook as it happens: the append-only file. The notebook lies on the desk, and once a second the clerk files the new pages in a fireproof safe: fsync. If the clerk faints, the notebook is still on the desk and nothing is lost; if the building burns, only the pages in the safe survive. A second shop across town copies each change over the phone: the replica, always a moment behind, and the last few minutes of the call are recorded so a dropped line can resume where it stopped. The analogy breaks at the phone: a person who misses part of a call can ask what they missed in their own words, while a replica needs the exact missing bytes, and if the recording no longer reaches back that far, it throws its copy away and starts again from a fresh photo.
in_your_world: Before you touch these settings, decide what each Redis in the payment platform holds. The idempotency store and the rate-limit counters are data: give them `appendonly yes` with `everysec`, a replica or two, and Sentinel (or a managed service that does the same job), and configure the client with the Sentinel addresses, never with a fixed primary host. Then write down the windows that remain: about a second of writes on a machine crash, and a few seconds of unreplicated writes on a failover. Close them where it is cheap. Your payment provider accepts an idempotency key of its own and Oracle's unique constraint on the payment id stops a second ledger row, so a lost Redis key costs a duplicate request, not a duplicate charge. A cache of merchant profiles can run without persistence, but never as a primary that restarts automatically with replicas behind it: it restarts empty, and the replicas faithfully copy the empty dataset. If Redis runs in Kubernetes next to your Quarkus services, give its pod room for copy-on-write: with `maxmemory 7gb` in an 8 GB pod, the first BGSAVE under heavy writes can get the pod OOM-killed. And check `latest_fork_usec` once: at 10 to 25 ms per GB it is a pause every client sees, every time a save point fires.
mistake: The most common mistake is to read `appendonly yes` as "no data loss" and stop there. Three gaps remain. With the default `everysec`, a machine crash loses about the last second. Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose writes the old primary acknowledged and never sent; WAIT narrows that window and doesn't close it. And a network split can leave clients writing to an isolated primary whose writes are discarded when it rejoins as a replica. People make the mistake because the setting's name sounds absolute and because kill -9 tests pass, as they do in this lesson's lab. The fix is to name the failure you are protecting against. For a crashed process, AOF with `everysec` is enough. For a dead machine, add a replica, and WAIT or WAITAOF on the writes that matter. For a split, add `min-replicas-to-write`. And keep the final guarantee for payments in the database or at the payment provider.

compare.note: Both send SET and then WAIT on one connection, because WAIT measures that connection's last write. Jedis's `RedisClient` lends a pooled connection to each call, so two separate calls can travel on two connections, and a WAIT on a connection that wrote nothing returns at once: in the lab it answered 1 in 5 ms while the replica was frozen. The pipeline pins both commands to one connection. Lettuce shares one connection among all callers, so WAIT always follows the write, but WAIT blocks that connection: every other coroutine using it waits up to 500 ms behind it. Give code that calls WAIT a connection of its own. In both languages the answer is a count, and the code decides what a 0 means.

worked.title: Choose persistence and failover for the idempotency store

steps.say: Start from what a loss costs and from the failures you expect. A lost idempotency key lets one retried payment reach the payment provider twice, and the provider's own idempotency key catches that. So the target is: nothing lost when the process dies, about a second when a machine dies, a few seconds of risk during a failover. That gives the primary's config. The `# ...` comments are notes for you; put real comments on their own lines in a redis.conf.
steps.code:
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec            # process crash: nothing lost; machine crash: about 1 s
aof-use-rdb-preamble yes        # rewrites write a compact RDB base file
save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000    # keep snapshots too: one file to copy off the machine
maxmemory 4gb                   # on an 8 GB machine: room for copy-on-write during a fork
repl-backlog-size 256mb         # 4 MB/s of stream for about a minute of outage
min-replicas-to-write 1         # an isolated primary stops taking writes...
min-replicas-max-lag 10         # ...after 10 s without any replica's acknowledgement

steps.say: Run three Sentinels on three machines, each with the same lines. A quorum of 2 marks the primary down; the failover itself needs a majority of the three. Five seconds without an answer is a long GC pause or a dead host, not a blip.
steps.code:
sentinel monitor payments 10.0.1.10 6379 2
sentinel down-after-milliseconds payments 5000
sentinel failover-timeout payments 60000

steps.say: The service connects through the Sentinels and never names the primary. After a failover the client asks again and follows the new primary.
steps.code:
RedisSentinelClient redis = RedisSentinelClient.builder()
        .masterName("payments")
        .sentinels(Set.of(new HostAndPort("sentinel-1", 26379),
                new HostAndPort("sentinel-2", 26379), new HostAndPort("sentinel-3", 26379)))
        .build();
redis.set("idem:7f3a", "PENDING");                  // goes to whichever server is primary now
steps.alt_code:
val uri = RedisURI.Builder.sentinel("sentinel-1", 26379, "payments")
    .withSentinel("sentinel-2", 26379)
    .withSentinel("sentinel-3", 26379)
    .build()
val redis = io.lettuce.core.RedisClient.create(uri).connect().coroutines()
redis.set("idem:7f3a", "PENDING")                   // goes to whichever server is primary now

steps.say: A few writes must survive even a machine crash: say the record that a payout batch went to the bank. For those, wait until the write is fsynced on this server and on one replica: `WAITAOF 1 1 200` returns two counts. Pay the extra milliseconds only on these writes, not on every idempotency key. Lettuce 7.9 has no WAITAOF method, so the Kotlin version uses Jedis too.

lab.title: Measure what a crash loses, then model a replica catching up
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. All 17 fail: nine in `ReplicationBacklogTest`, a model that needs no Docker, and eight in `CrashProbeTest`, which start their own Redis container and kill its server process with `kill -9`. A shell loop in that container starts the server again on the same port, as systemd or Kubernetes would.
In `ReplicationBacklog.kt`, write `feed`: add the bytes to the offset, append them, and keep only the last `capacity` of them.

Write `psync` from its KDoc, then `promote`. Run `./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l09.ReplicationBacklogTest'` until all nine pass. Read the boundary test: why is offset 134 enough and 133 not?

In `CrashProbe.java`, write `write`, `count` and `persistenceStat`, then `snapshot` (BGSAVE, then wait for the child) and `writeThenCrash`. Run all 17 tests. The names of the three AOF tests are this lesson's table in code.
hints: The backlog's oldest byte has offset `offset - backlogLength + 1`. A replica at offset r needs bytes from r + 1 on, so it can continue when `r >= offset - backlogLength` and `r <= offset`.
The missing bytes are the last `offset - replicaOffset` characters of the backlog: `backlog.substring(backlog.length - missing)`.
`redis.info("persistence")` returns lines like `rdb_bgsave_in_progress:0`, separated by `\r\n`. Find the one that starts with `field + ":"`.
Every `CrashProbeTest` test writes a fresh `redis.conf` and empties `/data` before it starts, so a failed test never leaves keys behind for the next one.

drill.title: The PSYNC decision from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write `psync(replicaReplId, replicaOffset)` for a primary that has `replId`, `replId2`, `secondOffset`, `offset` and a `backlog` string: return CONTINUE with the missing bytes, or FULLRESYNC with the current ID and offset. Then name the two situations that force a full resync.

recap: Memory is the only live copy. RDB snapshots, the append-only file and replicas each trail it, and a crash loses exactly the writes that hadn't reached a copy.
BGSAVE forks: copy-on-write gives the child a frozen view while the parent keeps serving. The fork pause and the copied pages are the cost, and with save points a crash loses minutes.

The AOF passes every write to `write()` before the reply. kill -9 loses nothing under any `appendfsync`; a machine crash loses about the last second with `everysec`, nothing with `always`. Rewrites keep the multi-part log short.
A replica follows the replication stream asynchronously. After a break it sends `PSYNC <ID> <next byte>`: inside the backlog (1 MB by default) that is a partial resync, beyond it a full one.

WAIT counts the replicas that have this connection's writes and undoes nothing. Sentinel (three of them: a quorum to agree, a majority to act) promotes a replica and tells clients where the primary is.

quiz.q: A Redis with the default save points and no AOF takes 50 writes a minute. The process is killed with kill -9. What is the most it can lose?
options: Nothing: RDB is on by default
About the last second of writes
About 5 minutes of writes, around 250 payments
Up to an hour of writes
quiz.why: At 50 writes a minute, the first rule to fire is `300 100`: 300 seconds have passed and at least 100 keys changed (250 have). So a snapshot happens every 5 minutes, and a crash just before the next one loses about 250 writes. The `3600 1` rule matters only on a quieter server, and the one-second figure belongs to the AOF with everysec on a machine crash.

quiz.q: The VM running Redis loses power. Redis had `appendonly yes` and `appendfsync everysec`. What is lost?
options: About the last second of acknowledged writes: the ones still in the kernel's page cache
Nothing: every write was in the append-only file
Everything written since the last AOF rewrite
Only writes that were never acknowledged
quiz.why: Each write reached the kernel with `write()` before its reply, but the page cache lives in RAM, and a power cut empties it. Only what the background thread had fsynced survives: everything up to about a second ago. A rewrite doesn't change that, because the base and increment files together hold every fsynced write. "Nothing lost" is true for a process crash, not for a machine crash.

quiz.q: A replica was cut off for 3 minutes. The primary writes about 2 MB of replication stream per second, and `repl-backlog-size` is the default. What happens when the replica reconnects?
options: A partial resync with the last 1 MB, and the rest of the gap is skipped
A full resync: the backlog holds 1 MB of a 360 MB gap, so the primary forks and sends a whole snapshot
The replica stays disconnected until an operator runs REPLICAOF
A partial resync, because the replication ID still matches
quiz.why: A partial resync needs both conditions: the ID must match and every missing byte must still be in the backlog. 3 minutes at 2 MB/s is about 360 MB, and the backlog keeps 1 MB, so Redis starts over with a snapshot: a fork on the primary and the whole dataset over the network. A backlog of about 400 MB would have made it partial. Redis never applies half of a gap, because the replica would silently differ from its primary.

quiz.q: Your service sends `SET payment:42 settled` and then `WAIT 1 500` on the same connection. WAIT returns 0 after 500 ms. What is true?
options: The SET was rolled back, because no replica confirmed it
The SET is queued and runs once a replica is available
The primary now refuses writes until a replica returns
The SET is applied on the primary and visible to every client; no replica has confirmed it yet
quiz.why: WAIT only counts. The write was applied and acknowledged before WAIT ran, and nothing undoes it: in the lab the payment was still readable on the primary after WAIT returned 0. Refusing writes is a different feature, `min-replicas-to-write`, and it applies to later writes. Treat 0 as "not confirmed": alert, or WAIT again.

quiz.q: A read-heavy service reads idempotency keys from a replica. One key's TTL has just passed, and the primary's DEL for it hasn't arrived yet. What does `GET` on the replica return?
options: The old value, until the DEL arrives
An error, because replicas can't evaluate TTLs
nil: the replica hides keys whose deadline has passed, but leaves deleting them to the primary
nil, and the replica deletes the key and sends the DEL to the primary
quiz.why: Lesson 5's rule: replicas never expire keys themselves, because two servers' clocks would make their datasets drift apart. They do check the deadline on reads and answer as if the key were gone. The key stays in the replica's memory until the primary's DEL arrives in the replication stream. A replica never sends writes to its primary.

flashcards.front: What does BGSAVE do that SAVE doesn't?
flashcards.back: It forks: a child writes the snapshot from a copy-on-write view of memory while the main thread keeps serving. SAVE writes it on the main thread and blocks every client.

flashcards.front: What does a BGSAVE cost the parent process?
flashcards.back: The fork copies the page table on the main thread (48 MB for 24 GB of data; about 10 to 25 ms per GB on modern machines), and every page the parent writes during the save is copied: up to twice the memory.

flashcards.front: kill -9 under `appendfsync everysec`: how many acknowledged writes are lost?
flashcards.back: None. Redis passed each one to `write()` before replying, and the kernel still has it. Only a machine crash loses about the last second.
The newest part of the replication stream, 1 MB by default, kept by the primary so a reconnecting replica can get only the bytes it missed.

flashcards.front: When does a replica need a full resync?
flashcards.back: When the primary doesn't know its replication ID, or the bytes after its offset have left the backlog.

flashcards.front: What does `WAIT 1 500` return, and what doesn't it do?
flashcards.back: How many replicas acknowledged this connection's earlier writes, after at most 500 ms. It never undoes a write and doesn't make Redis strongly consistent.
A failover needs a majority of Sentinels. With three on three machines, the side of a split that has one Sentinel can't promote anything.

terms.plain: A compact file, `dump.rdb`, holding the whole dataset as it was at one moment; written by a forked child.
After fork, parent and child share memory pages; the kernel copies a page only when one of them writes to it.
A log of every write command, replayed at startup; since 7.0 a base file, increment files and a manifest.
The system call that waits until the disk itself holds a file's data, instead of only the kernel's page cache.
A random name for a primary's history and a count of bytes in its stream; together they name one exact version of the data.
The newest part of the replication stream kept in the primary's memory for replicas that reconnect.
A reconnecting replica gets only the bytes it missed, from the backlog, instead of a full snapshot.
A separate process that watches a primary and, with the other Sentinels, promotes a replica when the primary is down.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate says: "Our Redis has AOF turned on, so idempotency keys can't be lost." Explain when they can still be lost, and what each risk costs to close.
explain_back.answer: AOF makes Redis log every write, and Redis hands that log to the kernel before it replies, so if only the Redis process dies, nothing acknowledged is lost. That part is true. But with the default `appendfsync everysec`, the log reaches the disk itself only once a second, so a power cut or a kernel panic loses about the last second of writes; `always` closes that at a large cost in throughput, and `WAITAOF` can close it for the few writes that need it. Second, a single server is a single machine: if it dies for good, the AOF dies with it, so we need a replica. Replication is asynchronous, so when Sentinel promotes the replica, writes the old primary acknowledged but hadn't sent yet are gone; `WAIT` after an important write tells us whether a replica has it, but it doesn't undo or block anything. Third, in a network split, clients cut off with the old primary keep writing to it, and those writes are thrown away when it rejoins as a replica; `min-replicas-to-write` makes it refuse writes after a few seconds. So the honest statement is: we lose nothing on a process crash, about a second on a machine crash, and a few seconds' worth on a failover or a split. For payments we close the rest outside Redis, with the provider's idempotency key and the unique constraint in the database.

deeper.body:
**Online backups in Redis 8.10.** `BACKUP START` produces a fresh base snapshot whether or not the AOF is on, `BACKUP SEAL` freezes the writes since then into an increment file plus a manifest, and `BACKUP LIST` names the files to copy, all without pausing writes or touching the server's own AOF rewrites. In the lab, `BACKUP LIST` after the seal printed `/data/backupdir/appendonly.aof.3.base.rdb`, `appendonly.aof.3.incr.aof` and `appendonly.aof.manifest`, and a second server started with `--preload-file aof:/tmp/restore/appendonly.aof.manifest` came up with every key, including one written after `BACKUP START`. `BACKUP CLEANUP` releases the files. Before 8.10, the safe way to copy an AOF directory was to switch off automatic rewrites while you copy.

**A truncated log.** If the server dies in the middle of a `write()`, the last command in the increment file can be cut off. With the default `aof-load-truncated yes`, Redis drops the broken tail, logs `!!! Truncating the AOF at offset ...`, and starts. Corruption in the middle of the file is different: Redis refuses to start, and `redis-check-aof` shows where it is.

**The newer full sync.** The lab's logs mention `rdb-channel`. Redis 8.0 changed how a full sync runs: the snapshot travels on its own connection while the replica buffers the live stream itself, so the primary no longer holds every write made during a long transfer. Valkey has a similar dual-channel replication. Either way the cost you plan for is the same: one fork and one copy of the dataset per full sync.

**A primary without persistence.** Some teams turn persistence off on the primary and keep it on a replica, to save the primary's disk. The replication docs warn about the trap: if the primary restarts automatically, it comes back empty, and its replicas sync with it and become empty too. Either keep persistence on the primary or make sure it never restarts on its own.

**Reading from replicas.** A replica answers reads by default even while its link is down (`replica-serve-stale-data yes`), so a read there can be seconds or minutes old. For idempotency checks, read the primary.

**Where this goes next.** The Replication track works through the general versions of these trade-offs: synchronous and asynchronous followers, failover, and the read guarantees a lagging copy breaks. Its lessons on leaderless replication and conflicts show what systems do when "last failover wins" isn't good enough.
